title: SLO Sensitivity & Simulation Lab Guide
author: Maya Patel
summary: Step-by-step playbook to design, run, and analyze SLA/SLO sensitivity experiments against the Redwood inference runtime using controlled synthetic traffic and observable perturbations.
content:
Overview:
This guide describes a repeatable lab for measuring how platform SLOs (latency, availability, error-rate, and token cost) react to incremental workload and resource perturbations. The lab is intended for platform engineers, operators, and reliability-focused on-call teams. The goal is to produce SLO sensitivity curves, a reproducible scenario catalog, and actionable runbooks for safe production rollouts and automated mitigations.

Why this lab exists:
- SLO targets are economic and operational knobs: a 50 ms median improvement may cost X percent more in GPU-hours.
- Teams need empirical mappings from workload characteristics to SLO burn rate to prioritize mitigations and capacity buys.
- Controlled, observable experiments reduce blast radius when designing fallbacks, model variants, or prefetch rules.

Scope and constraints:
- Scope: inference frontend + routing + runtime backends (GPU pools, KV cache).
- Excludes: tenant data plane-only issues (storage), model quality regressions (handled in evals).
- Lab must run in a non-production sandbox region or in production with tenant-flagged synthetic tenants and strict quotas.

Quick start checklist (preconditions):
1) Active sandbox cluster or isolated production tenant with:
   - Dedicated GPU pool (label: lab-gpu-pool)
   - Instrumentation: request traces, token-level billing, prefix/KV cache hit metrics, and per-model kernel telemetry
   - Synthetic-tenant API key and quota guardrails (max tokens/minute)
2) CI runner or controller with permissions to schedule synthetic traffic jobs and ephemeral feature flags
3) Template dashboards available (create from dashboard templates section below)

Environment matrix (table):
| Dimension | Low | Medium | High | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Sequence length | 32 | 128 | 1024 | Use realistic token distributions (see prompt-sets) |
| Concurrency | 1 | 8 | 64 | Scale concurrency independently from RPS |
| Cache hit-rate | 90% | 60% | 10% | Control via prefix diversity |
| Quantization | fp16 | int8 | mixed | Runtime kernel switch available |
| Burstiness | steady | periodic 10s spikes | Poisson bursts | Seed RNG for reproducibility |

Scenario definitions (DSL snippet):
- We use a simple YAML scenario DSL stored in /labs/slo-sensitivity/scenarios/*.yaml. Example: 

---
name: high-seq-low-cache
sequence_length: 1024
concurrency: 32
rps: 200
cache_prefixes: 0.9
quantization: int8
duration: 30m
abort_on: slo_burn_rate>0.25
---

Procedure: running a baseline sensitivity sweep
1) Provision lab resources: create lab-gpu-pool, isolate tenants, and tag running instances with lab=true.
2) Deploy baseline model variant (model: rdx-llama-7b-v1, kernels: optimized).
3) Start metrics pipeline: ensure traces and token-cost exporters are streaming to the lab prometheus/tempo/grafana stack.
4) Validate baseline traffic: run a 10-minute warmup at medium sequence and concurrency; confirm cache hit-rate and kernel selection.
5) Launch parameter sweep: for each sequence_length in [32,128,256,512,1024] and concurrency in [1,8,16,32], run the scenario for 15 minutes and record: p50/p95/p99 latency, error-rate, SLO burn, token cost per request, and QPS.
6) Automated aborts: each scenario has an abort rule. If p99 exceeds 3x target or error-rate > 5%, abort and trigger teardown hooks.

Dashboard and alert templates to create (fields to include):
- SLO Sensitivity curve: X-axis = request QPS or concurrency, Y-axis = normalized SLO burn (0-1). Lines per sequence_length.
- Kernel utilization: per-GPU kernel type counts, mem bandwidth, and %time-blocked.
- Token cost breakdown: tokenization, generation, KV lookup, network egress.
- Prefix cache cohort heatmap: rows=prefix, cols=hit_ratio over time.
- Scenario health panel: current scenario, start time, abort triggers, last checkpoint.
- Alerts to create (recommended):
  - slo-burn-rate-warning: fires at slo_burn_rate>0.5 for 5m in lab namespace (severity=warning).
  - lab-resource-exhaustion: GPU utilization > 95% sustained for 2m (severity=critical).
  - synthetic-traffic-leak: synthetic tenant traffic observed outside lab cluster (severity=critical).

Experiment variants and analysis guidance:
- Per-metric sensitivity: compute delta_slo/delta_load across axis. Use linear regression for small ranges; switch to piecewise polynomials when non-linearities appear (cache cold-warm transitions).
- Cost-normalized SLO: report SLO change per $1k GPU-hours. This helps product prioritize acceptable SLO loosening vs cost.
- Root cause decomposition: use causal tagging in traces (tag: kernel-version, quantization, kv-shard) and run an attribution algorithm to estimate contribution to latency.

Safe abort and rollback runbook (operator steps):
1) If abort on scenario triggers or a lab-critical alert fires: pause synthetic jobs via lab-controller: `labctl jobs pause --selector scenario=...`
2) Run quick triage: check p99 baseline on non-lab tenants, inspect kernel swap logs and OOM events.
3) If cross-tenant bleed observed -> immediately revoke synthetic tenant API keys and notify SRE on-call.
4) If isolated to lab scope: rollback model variant to previous stable image, run a 5m validation traffic, and only resume synthetic jobs once kernel utilization < 60% and p99 < 2x target.

Data collection and artifacts (what to save):
- Prometheus timeseries exports (raw) for all metrics touched
- Tempo traces for 100 sampled requests per scenario
- Kernel logs (nvprof-like output) and GPU telemetry snapshots
- The scenario YAML and job runbook (git commit hash)
- A screenshot of the SLO sensitivity panel and exported CSV of curves

Automations and CI integration suggestions:
- Lab scenarios are launched via a GitHub Actions workflow that checks out the scenario, runs preflight validators, and triggers lab-controller with a 1-hour TTL.
- Use `labctl` to orchestrate setup/teardown and enforce quota guards: `labctl run --scenario high-seq-low-cache --ttl 60m`
- Post-run job automatically uploads artifacts to the lab S3 bucket and opens a retrospective issue using a template.

Retrospective template (copy into postmortem issue):
- Title: [SLO-LAB] <scenario-name> - <date>
- Summary: one-line outcome and whether abort occurred
- Key metrics: p50/p95/p99 delta vs baseline, SLO burn, cost delta
- What went well: operator notes, dashboard clarity, automated abort success
- What surprised us: nonlinear transitions, cross-tenant signals, cache thrash behavior
- Action items (owner + due date): e.g., add kernel switch safety fence (owner: runtime-team, due: 2027-02-01)

Safety and compliance considerations:
- Never run synthetic tenant keys without quota and traffic egress caps.
- For experiments in production: require at least one approver from SRE and Privacy if traffic contains any customer-identifiable payload.
- All artifacts kept in the internal lab bucket for 90 days then archived.

Ownership and escalation:
- Lab owner: Platform Experiments (team alias: platform-labs@redwood.ai)
- SRE on-call: primary escalation for cross-tenant or infrastructure issues
- Runtime team: owner for kernel/quantization mitigations

Appendix A — Scenario catalog (starter list):
- small-seq-prefetch: low sequence, high prefetch ratio, measures prefix-cache benefits
- bursty-concurrency: Poisson bursts to measure eviction thrash and tail latency
- long-seq-kernel-swap: ramp sequence length to force kernel variant changes
- hybrid-cache-warm: start cold then ramp identical prefixes to measure warmup time

Appendix B — Example Grafana queries
- p99 latency (request): `histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_bucket[5m])) by (le))`
- SLO burn rate: `increase(slo_violation_count[1h]) / increase(request_count[1h])`
